sshKeys.title: SSH keys
sshKeys.subtitle: Local check: ~/.ssh, ~/.ssh/config, ssh-agent and consoles — no connection to servers
sshKeys.footer: The app only reads files. It writes to disk only via “Fix permissions” and “Create key”.
sshKeys.keysHint: Keys from {{dir}}, plus those set in consoles and in ~/.ssh/config
sshKeys.notUsedLong: No console and no Host in ~/.ssh/config uses this key
sshKeys.scoreHint: Score 0–100: algorithm and key size, +5 with a passphrase, −10 without
sshKeys.randomartHint: Visual fingerprint (as in ssh-keygen -lv): handy for comparing keys by eye
sshKeys.createHint: The key is created in ~/.ssh on this computer. It is not sent to any server: add the public key there yourself.
sshKeys.createBadName: Latin letters, digits and _ . - @, no .pub at the end
sshKeys.createClash: A file with this name already exists
sshKeys.createNoPassphrase: Without a passphrase the key file alone grants access to servers. Better set one — the app fills it in for you if you save it in the console.
sshKeys.createRemember: Save the passphrase: it cannot be recovered. You can store it in the console’s “Key passphrase” field.
sshKeys.configHint: {{path}} and files pulled in via Include — read only
sshKeys.hintNoPrivate: Only the public key (.pub) exists — login needs the private one
sshKeys.hintPerms: Permissions {{mode}}: ssh will reject the key, 600 is required (SSH keys → Fix permissions)
sshKeys.hintNoPassphrase: Key has no passphrase — the key file alone grants access
sshKeys.hintNeedPassphrase: Key is protected by a passphrase — enter it below, otherwise ssh will ask on connect

agentManyKeys.title: ssh-agent holds {{count}} keys
agentManyKeys.why: If a console has no own key or no IdentitiesOnly=yes, ssh offers agent keys one by one. After ~6 attempts the server drops the login: “Too many authentication failures”.
agentManyKeys.fix: Set a key for consoles and add -o IdentitiesOnly=yes to the extra SSH arguments, or remove unneeded keys from the agent (ssh-add -d).

configIdentityMissing.title: Host {{host}}: IdentityFile {{path}} not found
configIdentityMissing.why: ssh skips this key and tries others — login fails or uses a different key.
configIdentityMissing.fix: Fix the path in {{file}}, line {{line}}, or remove the line.

configNoHostCheck.title: Host {{host}}: server key check disabled
configNoHostCheck.why: StrictHostKeyChecking no or UserKnownHostsFile /dev/null — ssh will not notice a spoofed server (man-in-the-middle).
configNoHostCheck.fix: Remove these directives ({{file}}, line {{line}}). StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new is enough for new servers.

configForwardAgent.title: Host {{host}}: agent forwarding enabled
configForwardAgent.why: While you are connected, root or an attacker on the server can use your ssh-agent to log in to other servers with your keys.
configForwardAgent.fix: Remove ForwardAgent ({{file}}, line {{line}}). Use ProxyJump to hop through an intermediate server.

configForwardAgentAll.title: Agent forwarding enabled for all hosts
configForwardAgentAll.why: ForwardAgent in Host * (or before the first Host) exposes your ssh-agent to every server you log in to.
configForwardAgentAll.fix: Remove ForwardAgent from the common block ({{file}}, line {{line}}); if needed, enable it only for a specific trusted host.

consoleDangerWeakKey.title: Production console “{{console}}” uses unprotected key {{key}}
consoleDangerWeakKey.why: The console is marked as production, but its key has no passphrase or is weak: whoever gets the key file gets production.
consoleDangerWeakKey.fix: Set a passphrase on the key (ssh-keygen -p -f <key>) and save it in the console, or use a separate ED25519 key with a passphrase for production.

consoleDefaultKeys.title: “{{console}}”: no key set
consoleDefaultKeys.why: ssh tries the default keys ({{count}} in ~/.ssh) and every agent key — the settings do not show which key is used.
consoleDefaultKeys.fix: Set a key in the console settings so it is clear which key is used where.

consoleForwardAgent.title: “{{console}}”: agent forwarding (-A)
consoleForwardAgent.why: While the session is open, root or an attacker on the server can use your ssh-agent.
consoleForwardAgent.fix: Remove -A / ForwardAgent=yes from the extra SSH arguments; use -J (ProxyJump) to hop through a server.

consoleKeyMissing.title: “{{console}}”: key file not found
consoleKeyMissing.why: The console points to {{path}}, but the file does not exist — ssh goes on without it or asks for a password.
consoleKeyMissing.fix: Choose an existing key in the console settings.

consoleKeyNoPrivate.title: “{{console}}”: only the public key exists
consoleKeyNoPrivate.why: Login needs the private key, but {{path}} has only a .pub and the key is not in the agent.
consoleKeyNoPrivate.fix: Point to the private key (the file without .pub) or load the key into the agent.

consoleNoHostCheck.title: “{{console}}”: server key check disabled
consoleNoHostCheck.why: StrictHostKeyChecking=no or UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null in extra arguments — ssh will not notice a spoofed server.
consoleNoHostCheck.fix: Remove these options. The app already accepts new servers automatically (accept-new).

consolePassphraseMissing.title: “{{console}}”: passphrase for {{key}} not saved
consolePassphraseMissing.why: The key is encrypted and not in the agent — ssh will ask for the passphrase on every connect.
consolePassphraseMissing.fix: Enter the passphrase in the “Key passphrase” field — the app fills it in for you.

consolePassphraseUnused.title: “{{console}}”: passphrase saved, but {{key}} is not encrypted
consolePassphraseUnused.why: This key does not need a passphrase — the key was probably replaced or its protection removed.
consolePassphraseUnused.fix: Check that the right key is set; if it is, set a passphrase on it or clear the “Key passphrase” field.

consolePasswordOnly.title: “{{console}}”: password-only login
consolePasswordOnly.why: A password can be guessed or captured by a spoofed server; a key is stronger and never sent to the server.
consolePasswordOnly.fix: Create a key, add it to the server and set it in the console (the password can stay as a fallback).

keyDsa.title: {{key}}: DSA key
keyDsa.why: DSA is considered insecure and disabled since OpenSSH 7.0 — many servers will reject it.
keyDsa.fix: Create an ED25519 key and replace this one with it.

keyDuplicate.title: {{key}}: the same key is also in {{others}}
keyDuplicate.why: One key under several names: easy to change the passphrase or permissions of one file and forget the other.
keyDuplicate.fix: Keep one file and use it in all consoles.

keyMultiWorkspace.title: {{key}}: used in {{count}} workspaces
keyMultiWorkspace.why: One key opens servers from different zones (personal, work, clients): leaking one file opens everything, and access cannot be revoked for just one zone.
keyMultiWorkspace.fix: Use one key per trust zone (e.g. per workspace) and move consoles over gradually.

keyNoPassphrase.title: {{key}}: no passphrase
keyNoPassphrase.why: The key file is ready-made access: a stolen laptop, a backup or malware gets into every server with this key.
keyNoPassphrase.fix: ssh-keygen -p -f {{path}} — set a passphrase (nothing changes on servers), then save it in the consoles.

keyPermsOpen.title: {{key}}: permissions {{mode}} — ssh will reject the key
keyPermsOpen.why: The private key is readable by others. ssh refuses to use it (“UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE”), and other users on the system can read it.

keyPrivateMissing.title: {{key}}: private key missing
keyPrivateMissing.why: The key is set in a console or ~/.ssh/config, but only the .pub exists and it is not in the agent — it cannot be used to log in.
keyPrivateMissing.fix: Restore the private key or point to another one.

keyRsa2048.title: {{key}}: RSA 2048
keyRsa2048.why: Still acceptable, but this size is considered aging; ED25519 is shorter, faster and stronger.
keyRsa2048.fix: Use ED25519 for new servers and replace this key when convenient.

keyRsaShort.title: {{key}}: RSA {{bits}} — too short
keyRsaShort.why: RSA below 2048 bits is insecure; modern OpenSSH rejects such keys.
keyRsaShort.fix: Create an ED25519 key and replace this one with it.

keyUnreadable.title: {{key}}: could not be parsed
keyUnreadable.why: The file looks like a key but could not be read: {{error}}.

keyUnused.title: {{key}}: not used
keyUnused.why: The key is not set in any console or in ~/.ssh/config. Forgotten keys are an extra risk.
keyUnused.fix: If the key is not needed, delete it (and remove it from servers where it is authorized); otherwise set it in consoles.

sshDirPerms.title: {{path}}: permissions {{mode}}
sshDirPerms.why: The key folder is accessible to other users, and ssh may refuse to read a config with such permissions.
